deep.reconstruction:
Heading: 'Reste von Quadraten' (residues of squares), with a column headed 'Divisor'. For each modulus n from 2 to 46, Gauss lists the set Q(n) = { k^2 mod n : 0 <= k < n } in increasing order, always starting with 0. Composite moduli are included alongside primes. A hand-drawn staircase line separates the first column (n = 2..32) from the second (n = 33..46). The table continues on the next page with n = 47..64.

Method (implicit; my reconstruction): it is enough to square k = 0..floor(n/2), because (n-k)^2 ≡ k^2 (mod n), and reduce mod n. Equivalently, by the Chinese remainder theorem, Q(n) is the product of the residue sets for the prime-power factors of n. As a consistency check, |Q(n)| is multiplicative, and |Q(p)| = (p+1)/2 for odd primes p. For example:
- |Q(39)| = 2·7 = 14;
- |Q(44)| = 2·6 = 12;
- |Q(46)| = 2·12 = 24, where the listed entries are R23 ∪ (R23 + 23).

The table is a working aid for problems of the Disquisitiones Arithmeticae type (sections IV and VI). Examples are deciding the solvability of x^2 ≡ a (mod n) and excluding candidate values in factoring, or in representation by quadratic forms. It has no connection to the least-squares elimination on the previous page.

I recomputed every row independently. Rows n = 2..38, 40..43, 45 and 46 are exactly correct. In row 15 the cancelled '5' and in row 35 the cancelled '34' are correctly deleted non-residues.
errors: n = 39: the list has 24 in place of 22. The correct set is {0,1,3,4,9,10,12,13,16,22,25,27,30,36}. 22^... check: 8^2 = 64 ≡ 25 and 10^2 = 100 ≡ 22 (mod 39), so 22 is a residue. 24 is not: 24 ≡ 11 (mod 13), and 11 is a non-residue mod 13. The entry count (14) is right, so this is a single substitution slip, unless the handwritten '24' is really a malformed '22'.

n = 44: the list includes 31, which is not a square mod 44 (31 ≡ 3 mod 4). The correct set has 12 elements: {0,1,4,5,9,12,16,20,25,33,36,37}. The page lists 13. Faint dots near this line may mark the 31 for deletion; this is uncertain.

results.what: Table of quadratic residues (sets of squares mod n) for all moduli n = 2..46, including composite moduli; continued to 64 on the next page
results.modern_name: Table of quadratic residues modulo n
results.usually_credited_to: Such tables are classical (Euler, Legendre). Gauss published residue tables for primes in the Disquisitiones Arithmeticae (1801, Table II).

deep.surprise_reason: A routine computational table of squares mod n, of exactly the kind Gauss used and published in connection with the Disquisitiones. It contains nothing beyond elementary computation, plus two small slips (n = 39 and n = 44).
